newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf Canada CEO not afraid to make waves.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada CEO not afraid to make waves.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd.'s hostile takeover bid for Britain's Clyde Petroleum Plc was just the latest splash by a tough-talking and mercurial Texas oilman who has built a career out of making waves.

Gulf Canada chief J.P. Bryan created much the same sensation in London this week with the Wild West flair and rugged individualism that made the Houston-born executive an instant celebrity in Canada when he came North to rescue the then-stumbling firm two years ago.
Gulf Canada announced on Wednesday it planned a 105 pence ($1.72) per share hostile bid for Clyde, which was valued at 432 million British pounds ($720 million).
It was the international acquisition Bryan had been telling his investors about for months -- new core assets to complement Gulf's operations in Canada and Indonesia.
Analysts on both sides of the Atlantic said they believed Gulf would be forced to up its offer before closing the deal after Clyde shares rose to well above the bid price.
But the talk of rival bidders did not frighten Bryan, a one-time Wall Street financier and keen student of American frontier history who has been active in the energy industry for 28 of his 56 years.
In late 1994, the prospect of controlling then-plodding Gulf would have been enough to leave even the most wily oil veteran shaking in his boots.

But Bryan and his investment firm, Houston-based Torch Energy Advisors Inc. rode into Calgary, Alberta, armed with C$300 million ($219 million) in cash aimed at wringing every ounce of value from the company's underexploited assets.

Gulf Canada had been saddled with crushing debt as part of the Reichmann brothers' Olympia & York empire. It later came under the control of several banks that were left to pick up the pieces after O&Y's infamous failure.
The speed at which Bryan overhauled Gulf and rebuilt its corporate culture shocked employees, investors and Canada's tight-knit oil and gas industry alike.

After an initial restructuring in early 1995 that saw the company's workforce shrink, its executive suite culled and debt restructured, Gulf moved through a series of corporate and asset acquisitions.

It quickly absorbed small Canadian producer Mannville Oil & Gas, assets owned by Archer Resources Ltd. and the government of Alberta's stake in the huge Syncrude Canada Ltd. oil sands operation, which it later took public.

In the fall of 1995, Bryan took his first slug in Canada when he lost a bitter takeover battle for Czar Resources Ltd., a company controlled by often pugnacious Calgary oilman Robert Lamond. Lamond dodged Gulf's ambush by drawing a richer bid from Ranger Oil Ltd.

Bryan said after the Czar loss that Gulf's refusal to top Ranger's bid showed he was not about to overpay for assets. But this year, he made several comments in Canadian media suggesting Gulf could be poised to make an offer for victorious Ranger, a firm with extensive North Sea assets.

He is not afraid to make waves outside the oil business either. Earlier this year, Bryan created a national controversy by speaking out on the the delicate issue of French-speaking Quebec separating from the rest of Canada.
Directing his comments in a speech to Quebec sovereiegntists, he said: "If a small, isolated group of you want to go back to France, we'll get you a boat."

Thousands of phone calls flooded Gulf's offices, some voicing support for Bryan's comments which were unprecedented by a business leader, others incensed an American would dare comment on the highly emotional Canadian debate.
Bryan made no apologies for his remarks, saying he had every right to speak out on any issue that affected international investment in his company.

Another move, this time angering the residents of Calgary, was Gulf's recent announcement that 20 top executives -- including Bryan -- would pull up stakes and move to Denver, Colo. in 1997 to direct company affairs.
Still, few could argue Bryan's corporate alchemy and bombast have not spelled rewards for Gulf investors, who have enjoyed a doubling of their investment in the past two years.

"No question -- he has added a lot of value," said Martin Molyneaux, analyst with Calgary-based FirstEnergy Capital Corp. "In this town, since we're all so close together, we tend to think like a herd. This guy is no herd thinker. He does things his way and I find that refreshing."
